desc: Lockheed Martin is the company named more often than any other in the custody allegation, and the only one named on the floor of a congressional hearing by a sworn witness. Its documented government relationship is total: USAspending records show prime contract obligations to Lockheed Martin recipient entities running to the hundreds of billions of dollars since FY2008, spanning the F-35, Trident II D5, missile defense, national security space and classified aeronautics. It operates cleared facilities under DoD special access program accreditation, including Air Force Plant 42 at Palmdale and the Advanced Development Programs organisation that AARO's own historical report describes by name. The custody allegation attaches at three separate points. First, George Knapp testified under oath on 9 September 2025 that Robert Bigelow and an AAWSAP colleague negotiated with senior Lockheed Martin executives for a quantity of material 'stashed away and protected at a facility in California,' adding 'that material was not made here'; asked to name corporations holding material, he answered 'one of them is Lockheed,' and named a Lockheed executive as a gatekeeper. Second, Luis Elizondo testified on 13 November 2024 that an aerospace contractor sought to divest itself of material collected in the 1950s, confirmed the reported Lockheed-Bigelow transfer was blocked, and described a Secretary of the Air Force memorandum that never came. Third, AARO's Historical Record Report records - without naming companies - an interviewee claim that an organisation possessed off-world material in 2009 and 2010 and that a former senior CIA official quashed the proposal to remove it from the corporation. Lockheed Martin has issued no public rebuttal of the sworn testimony. AARO states that the executives and chief technology officers of the named companies met its Director and denied the allegations on the record.

claims.text: George Knapp testified under oath on 9 September 2025 that 'Robert Bigelow and a trusted colleague from AAWSAP met with and negotiated with senior executives at Lockheed Martin and hammered out a deal wherein Bigelow's company, BAASS, would receive a quantity of unusual material that had been stashed away and protected at a facility in California. That material was not made here.'
Asked by Rep. Tim Burchett at the same hearing to name the corporations holding the material, Knapp answered: 'Well, one of them is Lockheed.'
Knapp added at the same hearing: 'I am not saying Lockheed's the bad guys. They are doing what they were asked to do. ... They have lied about this because that is what they are supposed to do.'

Luis Elizondo testified on 13 November 2024 that 'there was an aerospace contract company that requested to divest itself of the material ... that was collected in the 1950s. Unfortunately, that did not actually occur.'

Asked at the same hearing about journalist Christopher Sharp's report of a transfer between Lockheed Martin and Bigelow Aerospace that the CIA blocked, Elizondo answered: 'What I can say is that it was blocked. Why it was blocked, I can only surmise. I was part of some conversations later on with some of those contract personnel where they had told all of us that is accurate.'
Elizondo testified at the same hearing that 'What we required was a memo from the Secretary of the Air Force in order to make that complete, and that never occurred.'

claims.text: 32 CFR 117.6(b)(3) provides that 'The Director, DCSA, will be relieved of this oversight function for DoD special access programs (SAPs) when the Secretary of Defense or the Deputy Secretary of Defense approves a carve-out provision in accordance with DoDD 5205.07' - the legal mechanism by which a cleared contractor facility can be removed from the government's standing industrial security inspection regime.

DoD Directive 5205.07, 'Special Access Program Policy,' effective 12 September 2024, states at Section 3.1.g that 'No DoD contractor entity, contractor employee, contractor representative, or consultant will provide SAP material to any members of Congress or their staff without Director, DoD SAPCO approval.'

10 U.S.C. 119(e) permits the Secretary of Defense to waive the inclusion of specified information in required SAP reports on a case-by-case national security determination, in which case the information and the waiver justification go only 'jointly to the chairman and ranking minority member of each of the defense committees.'

AARO's Historical Record Report, Volume I, records an interviewee claim that an organisation 'was in possession of off-world material in 2009 and 2010,' that a separate interviewee 'participated in negotiations to return the material to the USG,' and that 'a former named senior CIA official quashed the proposal to remove the material from the corporation.'

The same AARO report records a separate interviewee claim that an organisation held twelve spacecraft recovered from different crash events prior to 1970, some allegedly 'intact,' and that the CIA had a partnership with the company that ended in 1989.

AARO's stated basis for rejecting the corporate custody allegation is that 'The executives, scientists, and chief technology officers of the companies named by interviewees met with the Director of AARO and denied on the record that they have ever recovered, possessed, or engaged in reverse-engineering of extraterrestrial technology' - without naming the executives, the companies, the dates, or any verification step beyond the meeting.

Rep. Eric Burlison's 22 May 2026 interrogatories to MITRE list Lockheed Martin first among the entities whose UAP-related work MITRE must identify, placing the company's name in a formal congressional production request rather than only in testimony.

No contract, facility designation, transfer or shipping document, inventory record, subpoena, inspection report, or on-the-record corporate response from Lockheed Martin to the sworn testimony naming it has been placed in the public record.

dossier.denialPosture: Lockheed Martin has issued no public, on-the-record rebuttal of the sworn testimony of September 2025 naming it. The only denial in the documentary record is AARO's summary statement in its 2024 Historical Record Report that unnamed 'executives, scientists, and chief technology officers of the companies named by interviewees' met the Director of AARO and denied ever having recovered, possessed or reverse-engineered extraterrestrial technology.
dossier.narrative:
The Lockheed Martin allegation is unusual on this board because it is the one that has been made under oath, in a hearing room, with a company name attached. On 9 September 2025, before the House Oversight Committee's Task Force on the Declassification of Federal Secrets, George Knapp told the committee: 'It has been widely reported and suspected that Lockheed Martin is one of the contractors - the defense contractors, that has held this stuff, stored it away in secrecy, and tried to figure out how it works.' He then went further and put his own reporting on the record: 'I have confirmed on the record that Robert Bigelow and a trusted colleague from AAWSAP met with and negotiated with senior executives at Lockheed Martin and hammered out a deal wherein Bigelow's company, BAASS, would receive a quantity of unusual material that had been stashed away and protected at a facility in California. That material was not made here.' Later in the same hearing Rep. Tim Burchett asked which corporations hold the material. Knapp answered: 'Well, one of them is Lockheed.' He added a line that is, for the purposes of this map, more revealing than the accusation itself: 'I am not saying Lockheed's the bad guys. They are doing what they were asked to do. ... They have lied about this because that is what they are supposed to do.'

Ten months earlier, on 13 November 2024, Luis Elizondo had testified to the same transaction from inside the government side of it. Asked by Rep. Burlison whether the government or defence contractors possess technology, Elizondo said one reason his predecessor programme AAWSAP was trying to collect material of unknown origin was that 'there was an aerospace contract company that requested to divest itself of the material ... that was collected in the 1950s. Unfortunately, that did not actually occur.' Burlison then put the Christopher Sharp reporting to him directly - a transfer between Lockheed Martin, Bigelow Aerospace, and a CIA block - and Elizondo answered: 'What I can say is that it was blocked. Why it was blocked, I can only surmise. I was part of some conversations later on with some of those contract personnel where they had told all of us that is accurate.' He described the missing instrument: 'What we required was a memo from the Secretary of the Air Force in order to make that complete, and that never occurred.'

The official record does not name the company, but it does record the allegation. AARO's Historical Record Report, Volume I, logs an interviewee claim that an organisation 'was in possession of off-world material in 2009 and 2010,' that a separate interviewee 'participated in negotiations to return the material to the USG,' and that 'a former named senior CIA official quashed the proposal to remove the material from the corporation.' A separate entry logs a claim that an organisation held twelve spacecraft recovered from crash events prior to 1970, some allegedly intact, under a CIA partnership that ended in 1989. AARO says it found no empirical evidence for either. AARO's denial is procedurally notable in its own right: 'The executives, scientists, and chief technology officers of the companies named by interviewees met with the Director of AARO and denied on the record that they have ever recovered, possessed, or engaged in reverse-engineering of extraterrestrial technology.' AARO does not say which executives, at which companies, on what date, and describes no verification step beyond the meeting itself. Under this board's sourcing rule, that is an artefact of a statement, not evidence of the fact asserted.

What makes the allegation structurally survivable rather than merely unproven is the regulatory architecture around a company like Lockheed Martin. Industrial security oversight of cleared contractors is normally exercised by the Defense Counterintelligence and Security Agency under the National Industrial Security Program. But 32 CFR 117.6(b)(3) provides that 'The Director, DCSA, will be relieved of this oversight function for DoD special access programs (SAPs) when the Secretary of Defense or the Deputy Secretary of Defense approves a carve-out provision in accordance with DoDD 5205.07.' A carve-out programme is therefore a cleared contractor facility from which the government's own standing industrial security inspector has been formally removed by name, at the direction of the second-ranking official in the Department.

The congressional side is narrowed by the same directive. DoD Directive 5205.07, reissued 12 September 2024, states at Section 3.1.g: 'No DoD contractor entity, contractor employee, contractor representative, or consultant will provide SAP material to any members of Congress or their staff without Director, DoD SAPCO approval.' That is a standing prior-restraint on contractor-to-Congress disclosure inside the SAP world, in an unclassified, publicly posted directive. The statutory reporting channel is narrower still: 10 U.S.C. 119(e) lets the Secretary of Defense waive the content of any SAP report to the defence committees on a case-by-case national security determination, in which case the information goes 'jointly to the chairman and ranking minority member of each of the defense committees' - twelve people, not six bodies.

So the record on Lockheed Martin has an unusual shape. Two witnesses under oath, one of them a former Pentagon official, describing the same blocked transfer with the same missing Secretary of the Air Force memorandum. An official report that catalogues the allegation, does not name the company, and reports an unverified denial from unnamed executives. A statutory and regulatory framework that would make exactly this kind of holding invisible to the ordinary inspection and reporting machinery. And, on the other side of the ledger, no contract, no facility designation, no shipping document, no inventory, no subpoena, no inspection, and no on-the-record statement from Lockheed Martin responding to sworn testimony that named it.
openQuestions: Whether any Lockheed Martin facility has ever operated under a Secretary or Deputy Secretary of Defense-approved carve-out relieving DCSA of industrial security oversight, and if so for which programmes and over what period. Carve-out approvals are not published.
The identity of the 'facility in California' described in Knapp's sworn testimony, and whether it is a company-owned site or leased space on a government-owned installation.
Whether the Secretary of the Air Force memorandum Elizondo described as necessary and never issued exists in draft, and in whose files.
Whether Lockheed Martin executives were among those AARO says met its Director, and on what date - AARO names neither the companies nor the individuals.

Lockheed Martin's SEC filings report results attributable to classified programmes without identifying them; whether any of those programmes intersect the custody allegation cannot be tested from the public filings and is a line of research, not a claim.
dossier.whatItIs: Lockheed Martin Corporation is the largest single recipient of United States defense contract obligations, formed by the 1995 merger of Lockheed and Martin Marietta. It operates cleared facilities accredited for Special Access Program work and runs the Advanced Development Programs organisation, the Skunk Works, which has built the U-2, SR-71 and F-117 among other classified aircraft. It is the only corporation named on the record, by a sworn witness in a congressional hearing, as a holder of recovered non-terrestrial material.
dossier.whyImplicated: Lockheed Martin sits at the intersection of the two conditions this board treats as necessary for a legacy programme to survive without congressional visibility: a company with the industrial capacity to store and work on recovered material, and a legal regime that can lift normal industrial security oversight off it. Under 32 CFR 117.6(b)(3) the Director of DCSA is relieved of National Industrial Security Program oversight for DoD special access programs whenever the Secretary or Deputy Secretary approves a carve-out provision. Under DoD Directive 5205.07, no contractor employee or consultant may provide SAP material to any member of Congress or their staff without the approval of the Director of the DoD SAP Central Office. Two sworn witnesses - George Knapp in September 2025 and Luis Elizondo in November 2024 - have testified to a specific, dated, blocked transaction in which material collected in the 1950s and held at a California facility was to move from a corporation to Bigelow's BAASS, and did not. Lockheed Martin has issued no public rebuttal of that sworn testimony.

entityInfo.desc: Longer note on the state of the Lockheed Martin allegation as of August 2026. Four independent strands converge on the company and none of them has produced a document. (1) Sworn testimony: George Knapp, 9 September 2025, on the BAASS negotiation for material at a California facility and on Lockheed as one of the corporate holders; Luis Elizondo, 13 November 2024, confirming that the divestment of 1950s-collected material was blocked. (2) Official record: AARO's Historical Record Report catalogues, without naming companies, an allegation that an organisation held twelve pre-1970 recovered craft with a CIA partnership ending in 1989, and a separate allegation that an organisation held off-world material in 2009-2010 whose return to government was quashed by a former senior CIA official. (3) Legislative record: the Senate voted for federal eminent domain over recovered technology 'controlled by private persons or entities' and the Senate Intelligence Committee voted to compel contractors to inventory 'all non-earth origin or exotic' material; both provisions were stripped in conference. (4) Investigative journalism: Christopher Sharp's reporting, read into a congressional hearing by Rep. Burlison and confirmed by the witness. What is absent is equally specific: no contract, no facility designation, no shipping document, no internal Lockheed record, no subpoena, no inspection, and no on-the-record response from the company to the sworn testimony naming it. AARO says the executives denied everything on the record; AARO does not say which executives, at which companies, or on what date, and describes no verification beyond the meeting itself.
